trails.bestSeason: Oct-Apr (avoid extreme summer heat in the basin)
trails.trailTip: The final stretch is a slick-rock scramble down to the pour-off itself — use caution near the edge, especially when wet, since it's a sheer drop into the canyon below.
trails.didYouKnow: The "Window" is a pour-off in the Chisos Basin rim where all basin rainfall drains, framing a view straight out to the desert floor far below.

trails.bestSeason: Oct-Apr; can still be hot in the high country in summer
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, day hikes on this loop do not require a permit, but camping overnight at a South Rim backcountry campsite requires a free backcountry use permit obtained in person at park headquarters.
trails.didYouKnow: The South Rim offers sweeping views over the Chihuahuan Desert into Mexico and is often called one of the most rewarding vistas in the entire National Park System.

trails.bestSeason: Oct-Apr; the Terlingua Creek crossing can be impassable after rain
trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, the trail's initial Terlingua Creek crossing can be knee-deep or impassable after rain, so check current conditions at the visitor center before starting.
trails.didYouKnow: The canyon walls here rise over 1,500 feet straight up from the Rio Grande, and the trail runs directly along the U.S.-Mexico border for its entire length.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round; best Oct-Apr for cooler temps
trails.trailTip: One of the most popular day hikes in the park — arrive early to find parking at the small Panther Pass trailhead lot.
trails.didYouKnow: The first mile alone climbs to a saddle with views rivaling the full hike, making it a popular shorter turnaround for those short on time.

trails.bestSeason: Year-round; Rio Grande water levels affect the springs' depth
trails.trailTip: The trail passes an old bathhouse foundation and ends at a warm spring pool along the Rio Grande — the unpaved access road is rough, so check current road conditions before driving in.
trails.didYouKnow: The springs were the site of a small early-1900s resort where visitors soaked in 105°F water believed to have healing properties.

trails.bestSeason: Oct-Apr; afternoon thunderstorms common in summer at elevation
trails.trailTip: The final approach to the true summit requires a short, exposed rock scramble near the top — not recommended in wet or icy conditions.
trails.didYouKnow: At 7,825 feet, Emory Peak is the highest point in Big Bend and the second-highest in Texas outside the Guadalupe Mountains.

trails.trailTip: The trail follows the Rio Grande into a narrowing limestone canyon; a sand dune partway along can be soft walking, and swimming isn't recommended due to unpredictable currents.
trails.didYouKnow: Boquillas Canyon is the deepest and longest of Big Bend's three major river canyons, with walls rising over 1,200 feet.

trails.trailTip: A flat desert walk to a cluster of rock "chimney" formations with faint Native American pictographs at the base — view and photograph the rock art without touching it, since oils from skin accelerate its fading.
trails.didYouKnow: The volcanic rock chimneys were used historically as a landmark and shelter by both Native peoples and early ranchers in the area.

animals.whereToLook: Desert flats near park roads and the Rio Grande Village area
animals.viewingTip: Watch roadsides and open desert scrub with binoculars — roadrunners are often spotted dashing across trails and are easiest to see by their motion rather than by approaching.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite rarely flying, roadrunners can sprint up to 20 mph and are one of the few predators known to kill rattlesnakes.

animals.whereToLook: Chisos Mountains high country, especially around the Chisos Basin and Boot Canyon
animals.viewingTip: View bears from a distance with binoculars and never leave food or scented items unattended in the Basin — store everything in the provided bear-proof lockers, since a fed bear often has to be relocated or euthanized.
animals.didYouKnow: Big Bend's black bears recolonized the Chisos Mountains naturally from Mexico in the 1980s after the original population had been wiped out decades earlier.

animals.whereToLook: Desert scrub near campgrounds and washes throughout the lowlands
animals.viewingTip: Javelina herds are often encountered near campgrounds — admire them from a distance with binoculars and never feed them, since javelinas that associate people with food can become aggressive toward the next visitor.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite resembling wild pigs, javelinas are peccaries, a separate family, and rely heavily on smell since their eyesight is quite poor.

animals.whereToLook: Chisos Mountains backcountry trails, rarely near developed areas
animals.viewingTip: Sightings are rare and brief — if you see one, keep your distance, pick up small children, and back away slowly rather than approaching for a closer look or photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Big Bend has one of the healthiest mountain lion populations in Texas, though most visitors who see one only glimpse it for a few seconds crossing a trail.

animals.bestSeason: Late Apr-Aug (only present in the Chisos during breeding season)
animals.whereToLook: Boot Canyon and the Pinnacles/Boot Canyon Trail in the high Chisos Mountains
animals.viewingTip: This species breeds nowhere else in the U.S. outside the Chisos — scan the oak-maple canopy of Boot Canyon with binoculars and follow its song rather than approaching a singing bird too closely, since flushing a nesting pair from cover wastes energy they need for raising chicks.
animals.didYouKnow: Birders travel from across the country specifically to see the Colima Warbler, since the strenuous hike into Boot Canyon is the only reliable way to find one within U.S. borders.

animals.whereToLook: Cliffs near the South Rim and East Rim, viewable from a distance along the rim trails
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, the park closes a portion of the East Rim Trail (and campsites ER-4 through ER-9) from February 1 through May 31 to protect nesting peregrines, with technical climbing prohibited within a quarter mile of known eyries during that window — view any falcon you spot from the open rim trail with binoculars rather than approaching cliff edges near a nest.
animals.didYouKnow: Peregrine falcons are the fastest animals on Earth, reaching over 200 mph in a hunting dive, and Big Bend's canyon cliffs provide ideal nesting ledges.

animals.whereToLook: Paved and gravel roads throughout the park during the fall migration
animals.viewingTip: During the fall mating migration, watch for tarantulas crossing roads at dusk from your vehicle at a safe speed, and observe any tarantula on the ground from a couple feet away rather than picking it up — they're not aggressive, but a defensive bite or irritating hairs are best avoided.
animals.didYouKnow: The tarantulas seen wandering in fall are almost all males searching for mates; females spend most of their decades-long lives in a single burrow.

animals.whereToLook: Desert washes and brushy areas near lower-elevation campgrounds
animals.viewingTip: Look for gray foxes at dusk along desert washes with a red-filtered flashlight or binoculars from a distance — never leave out food to draw one in for a closer look, since this makes foxes bolder around campsites and puts them at risk.
animals.didYouKnow: Gray foxes are one of the few canid species that can climb trees, using curved claws to escape predators or reach fruit.
